Trump says last week's selloff "probably" drove his push to reinstate Jensen Huang, and "I made the deal" after phoning Nvidia's board; NVDA surged 31%.

Super Micro jumped 14% and the S&P 500 ETF gained 5% as Bloomberg's Eric Balchunas declared "Trump Put in effect.."

Even after the rally, Nvidia is down 26% over the month, and Trump's own Nvidia holdings make the put both durable and dangerous.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

President Trump went on CNBC Monday morning and said out loud what traders had long suspected. Asked whether last week's selloff factored into his push to put Jensen Huang back in charge of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), he answered: "Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term." He told CNBC's Eamon Javers he spoke to the board and "convinced them," adding, "I made the deal." Trump said he dialed into Nvidia's board meeting by phone and called his intervention "very important" to Huang's return.

Drew Angerer / Getty Images

A sitting president just described a reflex in his own words. When stocks fall hard enough, the White House picks up the phone.

Wall Street Priced the Backstop in Minutes

Nvidia climbed 31.31% in Monday's regular session, from $125.53 to $164.83, on pace for its biggest intraday gain since 2003, according to Hedgeye. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) rose 4.85%. Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI), whose server business lives on Nvidia's chip roadmap, gained 14.11%.

NVDA Price Scenario — 24/7 Wall St.

At 11:00 a.m. ET, Bloomberg ETF analyst Eric Balchunas named the trade: "Trump Put in effect.." He grouped it with the Fed Put and the Vanguard Put as reasons he stays bullish long term.

Super Micro Soars 20% on Report It's Seeking Up to 45% More for AI Servers Already Sold ©Oleksii Mach and yangwenshuang from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Super Micro rose 20% on a report that it and Dell want up to 45% more for AI servers already sold.

Making buyers cover memory costs would protect Super Micro's thin 12.0% gross margin.

A memory maker benefits if buyers pay up instead of trimming orders.

Dell's report Tuesday is the first test of whether customers pay.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) stock is up 20% today after the Financial Times reported Sunday that it, Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE), Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Lenovo are asking buyers to pay 25% to 45% more at delivery than their contracts say for Nvidia-based AI servers. They reportedly blame memory and circuit-board shortages.

Tech stocks rallied across the board after Nvidia's board voted unanimously this morning to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, with Nvidia up 33%.

Memory makers are collecting the difference. One memory maker brought in $4.8 billion of data center revenue in its quarter ended Oct. 2, up from $269 million a year earlier. Buyers who pay up rather than cut orders help it hold those prices.

Super Micro has the most riding on this

Dell, up 23% too, has shown it can pass costs along: after it raised server prices last December, its gross margin rose to 21.0% in the quarter ended July 31, from 17.9% the quarter before. Super Micro has more to gain, with analysts expecting its normalized EPS to jump 80% to $6.52 in fiscal 2027 (the year to June):

Super Micro Computer (SMCI): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2029 (years to June) (TIKR)

It has the least room of the group to hit those numbers, since its gross margin fell back to 12.0% in the September quarter, after 17.5% in June:

Super Micro Computer (SMCI): gross margin (%), last 8 quarters (to September 30, 2026) (TIKR)

On $19.9 billion of September-quarter sales, each point of gross margin is worth about $200 million a quarter. Passing memory costs along means Super Micro doesn't have to absorb them on deals signed at old prices.

TIKR tracks 18 analysts on Super Micro Computer. How many say "Buy"?

Priced for the worst

None of that is in the stock. Super Micro traded at 3.4x forward earnings at the last close, against a five-year average of 15x:

Super Micro Computer (SMCI): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Even after today's jump, it's under 4x.

Dell's Tuesday report is the first read on whether buyers will pay: it guides to $19 billion of AI server revenue for the quarter, against an AI backlog of $95 billion at July 31. Hitting the guide with the backlog intact would mean buyers are paying, good news for Sandisk (SNDK:NASDAQ) too. The risk is that debt-heavy AI clouds delay deliveries rather than pay 45% more.

Dell Technologies DELL is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Nov. 24.

For the to-be-reported quarter, Dell expects revenues of $49 billion, plus or minus $500 million, and non-GAAP earnings of $6.50 per share, plus or minus 10 cents. Dell's fiscal third-quarter results are expected to benefit from accelerating demand for AI-optimized servers, growing investments in traditional server infrastructure, improving enterprise storage demand and commercial PC refresh activity. Strong pricing discipline, operating efficiencies and an expanding AI infrastructure backlog are also expected to have supported profitability.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal third-quarter revenues is pegged at $50.87 billion, suggesting 88.4% growth from the figure reported in the year-ago quarter. The consensus mark for quarterly earnings is pegged at $6.76 per share, up 2% over the past 30 days. DELL reported earnings of $2.59 per share in the year-ago quarter.

Dell's earnings beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate in all the trailing quarters, with an earnings surprise of 28.96% on average.

Consensus Estimate Trend

Let's see how things have shaped up for DELL shares prior to this announcement.

Dell Technologies Inc. Price and EPS Surprise
Dell Technologies Inc. Price and EPS Surprise

Dell Technologies Inc. price-eps-surprise | Dell Technologies Inc. Quote

Key Factors to Note Ahead of DELL's Q3

Dell's Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) performance is expected to have benefited from robust demand for AI-optimized servers, supported by accelerating investments from neocloud providers, sovereign AI projects and enterprise customers. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Dell secured record AI server orders worth $60.9 billion and exited with a backlog of $95 billion. The substantial backlog is expected to have supported third-quarter revenue conversion. Dell projected AI server revenues of approximately $19 billion for the to-be-reported quarter, compared with $16.4 billion in the preceding quarter. Growing demand for rack-scale AI systems, including NVIDIA Vera Rubin-based infrastructure, is likely to have strengthened ISG's performance in the to-be-reported quarter.

Dell's traditional server and networking business is likely to have benefited from accelerating enterprise data center modernization, increasing CPU requirements for AI inference and agentic workloads, and growing demand for enhanced cybersecurity and infrastructure resiliency. The business reported 122% year-over-year revenue growth in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, reflecting strong customer demand and market share gains. Enterprises upgrading aging server infrastructure to newer, higher-density systems are expected to have supported demand in the third quarter. The company's expanding portfolio of next-generation servers, coupled with its supply chain capabilities, is likely to have strengthened its competitive position.

Dell's storage business is expected to have benefited from increasing enterprise investments in data management, protection and AI-ready infrastructure. Growing adoption of its PowerStore, PowerScale, PowerFlex, PowerProtect and ObjectScale solutions is likely to have supported revenues. Rising adoption of AI inference applications, which require enterprises to store and process increasingly large volumes of data, is expected to have provided additional momentum. A favorable mix of Dell-branded intellectual property storage offerings is also likely to have supported ISG profitability.

Dell's Client Solutions Group (CSG) is expected to have benefited from continued commercial PC refresh activity, supported by enterprise IT modernization and growing demand for AI-capable devices. Demand from large enterprise customers upgrading aging PC fleets is likely to have supported the to-be-reported quarter top-line growth. Higher average selling prices and pricing discipline amid rising component costs may also have supported revenue growth. Dell expects CSG revenues to increase approximately 15% year over year in the fiscal third quarter.

However, Dell is facing supply constraints across DRAM, NAND, CPUs, hard disk drives and networking components. These constraints are likely to have limited Dell's ability to fully capitalize on demand during the third quarter. Higher component costs, particularly memory, could also have pressured profitability despite pricing adjustments. The rapid expansion of Dell's AI server business poses a profitability challenge because these systems generally carry lower percentage margins than enterprise storage solutions. The increasing contribution from AI servers could have weighed on overall gross margin rates during the to-be-reported quarter.

Today's big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?

Update, Nov 23: Nvidia stock rose more than 30%, to about $166, in Monday morning trading after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO; his resignation had been announced Nov. 12. The board's announcement does not mention the reported SEC review, and Nvidia's Nov. 17 results and outlook are unchanged. The figures below are at Friday's close, and at about $166 the stock still sits below the $185 base case.

Nvidia reported strong results on Nov. 17. Its sales for the quarter through October were $115.8 billion. Analysts had expected $109.3 billion. It forecast about $130 billion for the quarter through January.

On Friday, Nov. 20, Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported that enforcement staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. The stock was already down more than 6% by then, on a day chip stocks broadly sold off. It closed down 14% at $125.53.

The report is not a charge, and the SEC declined to comment. But it landed on a question that had been building for months. Can the handful of companies buying Nvidia's chips keep paying for them? And what is the stock worth if they can't? Trefis has worked through that question piece by piece in recent weeks. This article puts it all in one place.

Nvidia in four lines: what its buyers spend, what the forecast needs, and what $125.53 assumes

1

	

Five big buyers put $691 billion into capital spending over the past year. Nvidia's sales equal about 52 cents of each dollar.




2

	

Analysts' forecast for next year needs $1.38 trillion of that spending. The five can reach $1.27 trillion, and only by borrowing to the limit.




3

	

On cash alone, $125.53 is what an investor would pay if Nvidia's sales fell to about $373 billion and never grew again.




4

	

If the buyers cut back the way they did in 2002 and margins fall to 40%, the stock's floor is about $83. If the SEC news follows the middle of six past cases, about $92.

Source: Trefis. Buyers: Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, the past year to September 2026 (Oracle to August). Nvidia: the past year to October 2026. Forecast: analysts' consensus for the year to January 2028. Price: Nov. 20 close.

If the SEC news follows the middle of six past cases, Nvidia's stock would be about $92. If this one stock holds much of your savings, a drop like that hits your whole account. The Nasdaq just logged its worst weekly decline since 2020, falling roughly 10% last week as doubts over artificial intelligence (AI) profitability set off a broad tech rout. Anthropic's record IPO gave back much of its opening pop, and NVIDIA slid more than 20% last week amid an SEC probe and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation.

The selling spread into AI infrastructure plays, including power, networking, optical and data-center names, where pullbacks may reflect sentiment rather than weakening demand. Still, the AI revolution shows few signs of slowing. For investors willing to take a chance with a multi-year horizon, the selloff could create buying opportunities.

Five AI infrastructure stocks that pulled back sharply last week and could be worth buying now include data center cooling and power play Vertiv Holdings VRT, down 19.4%; data storage provider Western Digital WDC, down 11.6%; AI server builder Super Micro Computer SMCI, down 19%; optical networking supplier Coherent Corp. COHR, down 14%; and data center hardware manufacturer Celestica Inc. CLS, down 16%.

Let's see why these companies look like buying opportunities now.

Vertiv: The company sits at the center of one of AI's biggest bottlenecks— powering and cooling increasingly dense data centers. In the third quarter of 2026, net sales rose 61% year over year to $4.31 billion, including 55% organic growth, while organic orders more than doubled. Management raised 2026 sales guidance to $14.45-$14.85 billion, implying 37%-39% organic growth.

A growing pipeline across regions and larger, more complex multi-phase projects favor providers that can deliver at scale, giving Vertiv visibility into 2027 and beyond. Management expects capacity expansion and backlog execution to drive above-market organic growth in 2027.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Vertiv's 2026 and 2027 EPS has moved north over the past 30 days to $7.18 and $9.16, implying year-over-year growth of 71% and 36%, respectively. The stock currently sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy).

You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. 

Western Digital: The company's high-capacity hard drives offer cost-effective storage for the massive datasets behind cloud and AI workloads. In the fiscal first quarter of 2027, revenues climbed 55% year over year to $4.38 billion, with the Cloud segment making up 88% of sales and non-GAAP gross margin expanding to 58.1%.

Growth was driven by sustained demand for high-capacity nearline HDDs, including the initial ramp-up of its latest ePMR platform. Management expects fiscal second-quarter revenues of about $5.1 billion, up 66% to 72%, driven by robust exabyte growth and improved pricing. Its next-generation 44-terabyte HAMR drive remains on track to begin volume shipments in the first half of calendar 2027.
